source_read: PDF pp. 240–251 (all pages; Figure 1 map, Table 1 and Figures 3–4 checked on rendered pages) and the corrigendum, Medical Care Research and Review 2026, 83(4), pp. 299–300 (both pages). The article PDF on file already carries the corrigendum's changes 1–6 (corrected Methods passage, Table 1 and Figure 1 notes, added reference); its data-availability line reads 'modified as described' rather than '... in Appendix A'. Online Appendix A and the supplement were not read.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim is careful and correctly flags the abstract's 13.5%. Points it could add: (1) the number of observations (2,613 state-months in the whole-population model; 1,469 for Black residents; 4,455 cells in the triple-difference model) is below the 3,060 (51 × 60) and 12,240 (× 4 death types) a full panel would give, and the paper does not say which were dropped, so 'the 50 US states and the District of Columbia' is the frame, not the data used; (2) the paper does not say how the six map-only states were coded; (3) the event-study pre-period intervals (about ±0.15) are roughly twice the estimated effect (about −0.07), so the test of parallel trends is weak; the authors call pre-trends insignificant only for the whole population, all races and White residents, and the Black pre-period coefficients sit mostly at +0.1 to +0.2; (4) the fall appears at the month of enactment, which is hard to attribute to strips that must first be distributed and used.
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 3 (p. 248), 100(e^β − 1) with β ± 1.96 SE: whole population −6.67% (−11.65% to −1.40%) unadjusted, −7.13% (−10.70% to −3.42%) adjusted; all races −7.23% and −7.50%; White −7.41% and −7.96%; Black −11.93% and −8.42%. 100(e^+0.127 − 1) = 13.54%, confirming that the abstract's 13.5% is the unadjusted Black estimate with its sign reversed (the Results text gives 11.92%). Table 4 (p. 249): −5.16% and −5.45% (whole population), White −6.76% and −7.87%, Black −5.64% and −0.20% (−5.16% to +5.02%); Panel A reaches only p < .1 except Black (p ≈ .046). All match the claim. Absolute effect: against the counterfactual (3.03/e^β − 3.03) I get 0.216–0.233 fewer deaths per 100,000 a month, 2.6–2.8 a year, as in the claim; multiplying 3.03 by the percentage instead gives 2.4–2.6, so the figure is rough in the way the claim says. 3.03 is a mean over state-months with a law (Table 2) and the paper does not say whether it is population-weighted, while the models are. Table 1 has 16 jurisdictions (15 states and DC), from 1 June 2018 (Maryland) to 1 August 2022 (Louisiana); the map shades 22, and the six without dates are Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont and Wyoming. The text calls the outcome drug-overdose deaths; tables and figures call it 'drug-induced deaths'. Either way it covers all drugs.

anchors.extracted: Implementation dates for 16 jurisdictions (15 states and DC), 6/1/2018 (Maryland) to 8/1/2022 (Louisiana); dates are the authors' modification of NPHL dates.

anchors.locator: Figure 1 (map of FTS laws as of 2022)
anchors.extracted: 22 jurisdictions shaded legal; Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont and Wyoming are shaded but have no date in Table 1; their coding in the models is not stated.

State-month CDC WONDER mortality 2018–2022; outcomes: all drug-overdose deaths, and unintentional relative to suicide, homicide and undetermined overdose deaths; SEER population; log deaths per 100,000; NPHL dates used as preliminary information and modified, details in Online Appendix A.

Controls only for age profile (shares 18–34, 35–64, 65+), share living in rural counties (USDA codes 5, 7, 9) and median income; state and month-year fixed effects; Borusyak et al. (2024) estimator for staggered adoption; effects read as 100(e^β − 1)%.

anchors.locator: Method › Empirical Strategy, paragraphs after equation (2)
anchors.extracted: Triple-difference models use suicide, homicide and undetermined overdose deaths as controls for unintentional ones; all models weighted by state population; standard errors clustered by state.

anchors.locator: Results › Primary Results, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 244) and 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Unadjusted reductions 6.67% (written 'per 100,000 deaths'), 7.22% all races, 7.41% White, 11.92% Black; with controls 'somewhat stronger' except 'somewhat weaker' for Black; controls themselves not significant.
Mean drug-overdose deaths per 100,000 per state-month: 3.03 (SD 1.12) with FTS legal vs 2.37 (1.12) without; White 2.93 vs 2.47; Black 4.45 vs 3.37.

anchors.locator: Abstract; p. 241 New Contributions; p. 246 Discussion, 1st paragraph; p. 247 Discussion, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: About 7% fewer overdose deaths overall and 13.5% among Black residents, described as nearly twice the White reduction; 13.5% does not appear in Tables 3–4 (it equals the unadjusted Black coefficient with its sign reversed), and with controls Black and White estimates are similar.
Text calls the unadjusted triple-difference estimates statistically significant although three of four reach only p < .1 by the table's own stars.

anchors.locator: Results › Robustness Tests and Sensitivity Analysis, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Figures 3 and 4
anchors.extracted: Event studies without controls, 16 months before and 8 after; pre-trends called insignificant for population, all races and White; pre-period 95% intervals about ±0.15; Black pre-period coefficients mostly +0.1 to +0.2 and called more volatile; a sharp fall almost immediately at enactment.

State-level data may hide local variation; possible inconsistency in death classification across states; 5-year window; no measure of community groups supplying strips; strip use in states where they were illegal not considered; other state policies may affect overdose deaths.

Conclusion speaks of robust evidence of fewer opioid overdose deaths, particularly among Black populations; the Introduction states that FTS reduces overdose deaths. The outcome was deaths from any drug and the design is observational.
No conflicts declared; no financial support received.

Authors clarify that some NPHL dates were changed to mark the policy shock, documented in a new Online Appendix A; an Introduction sentence (21 states and DC legal as of 2024) deleted; Table 1 and Figure 1 notes revised; editor states results and conclusions unchanged.

key_findings.note: Recounted post-law months (law counted from the month it took effect, Jan 2018–Dec 2022): 362 in total, 236 in the five 2018–2019 adopters, as stated.

Checked on 300-dpi renders: in both Black panels every pre-period point is above zero (the lowest, about month −8, only just). In addition, several pre-period 95% bands lie wholly above zero (about months −11 to −9 and −4 in Figures 3 and 4), i.e. individually significant pre-trends; see 'missed'.

reporting_issues.note: 100(e^0.127 − 1) = 13.54% recomputed. The 'nearly doubled' wording is also on p. 247 (Discussion, 4th paragraph), not in this issue's page list.
Recomputed p from coefficient/SE: 0.098, 0.090 and 0.059 for the three starred p < .1.
Same six states in my own reading of the map.
Event-study axes read 'Months Relative to Enactment' on the renders.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with ROBINS-I, serious overall, for the whole-population estimate. For the Black-resident estimates the case for a more severe rating is stronger than the card states: several pre-period coefficients are individually significant (bands above zero), the authors do not claim flat pre-trends for this group, the model uses 48% of state-months, and the adjusted triple difference is null. The adjudicator may want a subgroup note or 'critical' for that estimate.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the miscomputed 13.5%, 'particularly effective' for unintentional deaths (actually weaker), 'robust evidence' of fewer opioid deaths (none analysed), and causal verbs about strips whose use was not measured.

missed.finding: Several pre-period 95% bands lie wholly above zero (about months −11 to −9 and −4 in both figures), so pre-trends for Black residents are individually significant. The text calls pre-trends insignificant only for the whole population, all races and White residents. This weakens the Black estimates beyond the card's 'every pre-period coefficient lies above zero'.
